newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines heads for debt issue watersheds.
newsitem.headline: Philippines heads for debt issue watersheds.

text.p: The Philippines marks another milestone in its economic revival on Tuesday when it issues its first fixed-rate, 10-year Treasury bonds in what will be a key test of investor perceptions of its long-term stability.

Riding the nation's new confidence and a string of positive indicators, several foreign fund managers have also started urging the Central Bank to allow the issue of peso-denominated bonds on the international market.

Financial analysts see both developments as watersheds for a country that re-entered international capital markets only four years ago after a 10-year hiatus, with the return of political stability and the implementation of economic reforms.
Bank treasurers said they expect the 10-year Treasury bonds to fetch a rate of 16 percent to 17.5 percent.
"Anything over 17 percent would be lovely. That would give a double-digit differential over the U.S. 10-year Treasuries," said Bank of America country treasurer Jaime Panganiban.
The 10-year bond issue comes at an opportune time, with domestic interest rates softening on tapering inflation, analysts said.

August inflation was 7.9 percent year-on-year, having fallen every month since last September when it shot to double-digit levels due to a rice shortage. Monetary authorities aim to bring it down to 6.0 percent by December.
As a result, the Philippines' 91-day Treasury bill rate, an interest rate benchmark, has slipped to 11.330 percent from a peak of 13.2 percent in May.

The government issued fixed-rate two-year notes in 1994, five-year notes in 1995 and seven-year bonds in early 1996. With the 10-year issue, it wants to provide a benchmark for long-term lending and lengthen the maturity of domestic debt as part of an overall plan to lower interest rates.

Since longer-termed paper was launched, the Bureau of Treasury said it has sold 15.585 billion pesos ($594.8 million) worth of the seven-year bonds, 38.680 billion pesos ($1.476 billion) of five-year bonds and 57.960 ($2.212 billion) of two-year notes.
Bureau of Treasury director Roberto Juanchito Dispo said in an interview the market response to the initial issue of the 10-year bonds would determine the frequency of future issues.
Cesar Zulueta, head of treasury in the Philippines for ING Bank, is optimistic about the new bonds. "Supply is not sufficient," he told Reuters.
ING, along with Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, has also been part of the lobby for a Europeso issue to foreign investors. The Central Bank is currently considering the proposal.
"We're looking at it. The Central Bank may have a decision before the end of the month," Treasurer Sergio Edeza said.

Fund managers say there would be high demand for the issue given the stability of the peso against the dollar in recent months, high domestic yields versus other markets and favourable ratings from international ratings agencies.

"The time is right for the Philippines," said Consuelo Garcia, deputy head for investment banking of ING Bank. She said ING was looking at a minimum issue of $50 million worth of three-year europeso bonds for some companies.

Morgan Grenfell wants a Europeso bond to be issued first by an international agency, such as the World Bank or the Asian Development Bank, to signal confidence in the Philippine peso as a liquid and convertible currency.
"The Europeso, from the regulator's point of view, is a big step since it would internationalise the peso," Bank of America's Panganiban said.

A Europeso issue would mean monetary authorities would have to be prepared for an increase in the peso's volatility, but sound foreign exchange management by the Central Bank could earn it high marks, Panganiban said.
"The Philippine Central Bank would be graduated into the league of emerging central banks in the likes of Thailand and Indonesia," he said.

Senen Matoto, executive director of BPI Capital Corp, said the economy was robust enough to cope with increased forex volatility. "But since the economy is doing OK, it's a good time to do it," he said.
A successful initial Europeso offering would encourage local companies to issue similar paper. Companies seeking funds overseas currently must issue dollar-denominated paper.
Local bank loan rates were hampered by a 15 percent reserve requirement that adds to bank intermediation costs, he said.

Analysts also said a Europeso note would attract more foreign companies to establish operations in the country since they will be able to access peso funding for their operations without having to worry about the need for capital hedging.
Moreover, a Europeso note would help international investors avoid the complications of tax issues on domestic bonds, they said.
